problem: RL/imitation navigation policies trained in clean environments fail to adapt at test time to unseen obstacles or perceptually deceptive objects (e.g., hanging cloth that LiDAR reads as solid), often freezing or colliding, and retraining is impractical.
motivation: Real-world deployment cannot cover all situations in training and learning from mistakes is unsafe. Human language feedback can resolve ambiguity, but the robot must know when to ask (sample-efficient queries) and how to turn free-form language into executable actions without large supervised data.
key_idea: Monitor ensemble-based epistemic uncertainty (mutual information) with Bayesian changepoint detection to decide when to ask a human for help, then use a zero-shot prompted LLM (GPT-3.5/Llama-2) to convert the language feedback into discrete action sequences that are executed before resuming the trained policy.
insight: Epistemic uncertainty is much more informative than action entropy, since multiple routes are equally optimal. The observation-space design strongly affects calibration: global-visibility and partial-global observations give spurious or misplaced uncertainty (qualitative figures), while goal-conditioned local observations give uncertainty spikes only near unseen obstacles (10-50x jump). In real-world tests, removing human feedback drops SR sharply (e.g., 80 to 10 in Scenario 3), showing that the feedback, not just the uncertainty trigger, drives adaptation.
method: Observation space design: compares global visibility, goal-conditioned local, and partial global observations; goal-conditioned local observation (local cost map + distance to goal) is chosen as it yields well-calibrated uncertainty.

Imitation-learned base policy: behavior cloning from expert demonstrations (Dijkstra paths in grid world; teleoperated Husky in obstacle-free simulation); random forest ensembles (500 trees) for tabular, CNN with MC-dropout for visual, PCA-reduced cost map for outdoor.

Epistemic uncertainty estimation: decomposes predictive entropy into aleatoric and epistemic parts; epistemic = mutual information I(a,θ|s,D), estimated as the difference between predictive entropy and expected ensemble entropy.
Query trigger: Bayesian online changepoint detection (Fearnhead 2006) on the per-step uncertainty stream to detect significant increases and request feedback, improving query efficiency.

Language feedback interpretation: zero-shot ChatGPT/Llama-2 prompted with the action-to-integer mapping converts free-form instructions into action sequences (e.g., 'go up 2 times then left' -> [0,0,3]) that are executed before the policy resumes.
Deployment: sim-trained outdoor policy transferred to a real Clearpath Husky with VLP16 LiDAR and evaluated against DWA and an ablation without feedback.

setting.backbone: Imitation-learned policy ensembles (random forest / CNN with MC-dropout / PCA-based net) + GPT-3.5 / Llama-2 (frozen, zero-shot prompting) for feedback interpretation
setting.training_data: Expert demonstrations only: Dijkstra shortest paths in grid worlds, and human-teleoperated goal-reaching trajectories (goals up to 20 m) in an obstacle-free outdoor simulator; LLM used zero-shot
setting.observation: Local robot-centric 2D cost map from LiDAR (obstacle layer + distance-to-goal layer, PCA-reduced) plus distance to goal; local grid / 100x100 images in grid worlds
setting.action_space: Discrete grid moves (up/right/down/left) in grid worlds; continuous linear/angular velocity (v, ω) for Husky
setting.simulator: Custom grid worlds (tabular and visual) and a high-fidelity outdoor ROS simulator with a Husky model; real world
setting.privileged: Human expert providing language feedback at test time (when queried); otherwise none

numbers_note: Only the real-world table (SR, normalized trajectory length) is quantitative; grid-world and simulation results are given only as figures. TL is labelled 'RL' in the caption but is normalized trajectory length. These are not standard VLN/ObjNav benchmarks.
results: In the real-world Husky tests, RE-MOVE reaches SR 100/90/80 in Scenarios 1/2/3 versus DWA's 100/100/0, and versus RE-MOVE without feedback's 40/30/10. It is the only method that succeeds when LiDAR shows no free space (tablecloth, Scenario 3), and it shortens trajectories versus DWA in Scenarios 2 and 3 (TL 1.134 vs 1.311 in Scenario 2).
limitations: Evaluation is small-scale and mostly qualitative: three custom scenarios, a single robot, and no standard benchmarks; the 'up to 80%' gain is only over DWA in one scenario.

Depends on a human available to give accurate feedback, and on a discretized action space for LLM translation; errors in uncertainty estimation and language-to-action translation lower SR (Scenario 2: 90 vs DWA's 100).
Requires careful observation-space design; global and partial-global observations give poorly calibrated uncertainty.
